summary: Unreal Engine is Epic Games' source-available real-time engine. Important correction to this project's subject record: version 6 has not shipped. On 17 June 2026 Epic released Unreal Engine 5.8 and, the same day, announced the plan for version 6; Epic's own documentation site carries 5.8 release notes and no version 6 documentation, and the community forum announcement dates the 5.8 release to that day. Everything below is scored against 5.8, the shipping engine. Verse is likewise not the gameplay language of the shipping engine: Epic documents Verse only under Fortnite and the Unreal Editor for Fortnite, and the 5.8 experimental feature list names no Verse or Scene Graph entry. In shipping Unreal the gameplay languages are Blueprint and C++. Epic's stated plan is to move the gameplay model to Verse for version 6, with early access targeted for the end of 2027, so a standards audience should treat Verse today as a language you can only run inside Epic's own Fortnite service, not as a portable engine feature. What the engine covers very well: rendering, geometry, physics, sound, packaging and, unusually, an open standard for immersive sessions, because head-mounted display support goes through the OpenXR plugin. What it does not cover is portability. The renderer's virtualized geometry system uses, in Epic's own words, an internal mesh format; the lighting system is an engine-private algorithm; and the built-in networking is the deepest lock-in of all, because replication is welded to the engine's own object model, its own wire protocol and matching client and server builds. The trap for a standards group is that almost every capability here is present and strong, and almost none of it is specified anywhere a second implementation could follow. The three places Unreal genuinely meets the outside world are OpenXR for sessions, the glTF importer and exporter for models, and Pixel Streaming, which sends rendered frames and sound to a plain web browser over WebRTC and so lets a cloud-rendered topology reach clients that could never run the engine.

coverage.note: The engine ships deferred and forward rendering paths for desktop and for head-mounted displays, plus a separate mobile path; the pass structure and render graph are engine-internal and are not published as anything a second implementation could follow.

coverage.note: Correction: this row previously asserted that the engine has no shared or persistent anchor model of its own. That is wrong. ARPin is the engine's own cross-platform anchor API, with a separate implementation behind it per platform; storing pin data locally persists content between app sessions, and cloud storage shares it between devices. Scored via-extension rather than native because persistence and sharing both arrive through platform plugins - Azure Spatial Anchors, ARCore Cloud Anchors, ARKit Geo Anchors - and the support matrix differs per platform, so an anchor is not portable across them.

coverage.note: Sign-in to Epic's service checks that the person has consented to the scopes an application requests, and refuses the login with a stated error when they have not. The consent is held by Epic's service and carries no purpose, expiry or withdrawal record that travels with the person.

sources.title: Online Subsystem EOS Plugin in Unreal Engine
sources.quote: The user has not consented to required scopes.

coverage.note: Games grant content according to entitlements that a purchase or a redeemed code gives the player, so use is gated on a held right. The right is a store record, and the engine does not read licence terms attached to an asset.

sources.title: Commerce Interface in Unreal Engine
sources.quote: Once the transaction is complete, the interface will grant the player the appropriate entitlements.

coverage.note: Two key mechanisms exist: encryption keys for packaged content, and a game-specific key that encrypts player data sent to Epic's online service. Both use a single key per game rather than key material identifying an intended recipient.

sources.title: Online Subsystem EOS Plugin in Unreal Engine
sources.quote: A 64-byte hexadecimal string that encrypts data when uploaded to an EOS service.

sources.title: Project Section of the Unreal Engine Project Settings
sources.quote: The default encryption key used to protect .pak files.

coverage.note: A game server decides whether to let a joining player in before the player is created, and a refusal carries a message the player receives. There is no validity limit on the decision, and the answer is a function in the game's own code rather than a defined response format.

sources.title: AGameModeBase::PreLogin
sources.quote: When set to a non-empty value, the player will be rejected using the error message set

coverage.note: The engine has no inventory of its own. The online interfaces let a game fetch the list of entitlements a user already holds from the store, so held items live with the store provider and travel only as far as that provider's catalogue does.

sources.title: Commerce Interface in Unreal Engine
sources.quote: Fetch the list of already acquired entitlements for the specific user from the store and cache them in the interface.

coverage.note: The user file interface lets a game read a person's configuration and save files from the platform's online back end, so settings can follow the person across devices for that game. The files are per game and the format is the game's own, so nothing follows the person to another application.

sources.title: User File Interface in Unreal Engine
sources.quote: Your game might require you to read user files that are not packaged with your title. Examples may include configuration files or user-specific game save files.

coverage.note: Sparse volume textures hold voxel volumes with several data channels, including animated sequences, and are filled by importing OpenVDB files. The data is converted into the engine's own format on import, doubles are reduced to smaller types, and the documentation describes no export back to a volume format.

sources.title: Sparse Volume Textures in Unreal Engine
sources.quote: You can import Sparse Volume Textures from VDB (or Voxel Data Base) files. This format is widely used to store sparse volume data.

coverage.note: Unreal saves an asset's thumbnail inside the asset's package, and a package holds a thumbnail map, so a preview does travel with the asset. It sits in Unreal's own package format and is read back through engine calls, not referenced or exported as a standalone image that another tool can use without opening the package.

sources.title: ThumbnailTools::AssetHasCustomThumbnail
sources.quote: Returns true if the given asset has a custom thumbnail cached or on the disk.

sources.title: ThumbnailTools::GenerateThumbnailForObjectToSaveToDisk
sources.quote: Used to generate the thumbnail that gets saved in a package.

sources.title: UPackage::GetThumbnailMap
sources.quote: Returns the thumbnail map for this package

coverage.note: The Variant Manager records alternative states of a scene, such as which objects are shown, which materials apply and which lights are on, apart from the scene content, and the glTF exporter can write material variants. Variants name specific objects; there are no rules that select features from content metadata.

sources.title: Working with Scene Variants in Unreal Engine
sources.quote: Unreal Engine offers a helper called the Variant Manager

sources.title: How the glTF Exporter Handles Unreal Engine Content
sources.quote: The glTF exporter uses the KHR_materials_variants extension to export Level Variant Sets.

coverage.note: Any asset can carry free-form key and value metadata, which could record a creator or intended usage, but the engine defines no licence key and the metadata cannot be read by gameplay code at run time. Nothing states what a recipient may do with the asset in a form a tool can act on.

sources.title: Asset Metadata in Unreal Engine
sources.quote: For example, metadata could include things like the name of the Asset's creator, the intended usage of the Asset in your Project, or the status of the Asset in your team's workflow

coverage.note: Searched the Unreal Engine 5.8 documentation pages reachable from its index (157 pages read, not the whole documentation set), the glTF exporter page and web search of dev.epicgames.com for provenance, C2PA, content credentials, signed authorship, asset signing on 2026-10-20; found no signed record of who made an asset. Metadata can hold an unsigned creator name, and packaged files can be signed only to detect tampering, which names no author.

sources.title: Asset Metadata in Unreal Engine
sources.quote: For example, metadata could include things like the name of the Asset's creator, the intended usage of the Asset in your Project, or the status of the Asset in your team's workflow

coverage.note: Searched the Unreal Engine documentation pages Using Live Link Data, Live Link in Unreal Engine and Enhanced Input (en-us, 2026-10-20) for heart, biometric, physiolog and sensor; no body-signal source type found, and a web search restricted to dev.epicgames.com and unrealengine.com found no first-party document. Live Link is a general streaming path that could carry such data, but the documentation describes no physiological source. The full documentation set was not searched.

sources.title: Using Live Link Data in Unreal Engine
sources.quote: Live Link provides users with the ability to stream various types of data from a variety of sources and apply that data directly to Actors within their level.

coverage.note: The experimental Unreal MCP plugin, with the All Toolsets plugin, runs an MCP server in the Editor so outside agents can spawn actors, set lighting, make material instances and run tests; what an agent can do is set by the enabled toolsets. By default it accepts local connections only and has no authentication layer. Missing: no publish step is described, so it covers creating and changing content in the Editor but not publishing it.

sources.title: Unreal MCP in Unreal Editor
sources.quote: Unreal MCP embeds an MCP server inside the Unreal Editor process so that any MCP-compatible AI agent, such as Claude Code, Cursor, or the MCP Inspector, can drive the editor over a local HTTP connection.

sources.title: Unreal MCP in Unreal Editor
sources.quote: By default, the server only accepts connections from the same machine, has no authentication layer, and is not designed for remote use.

coverage.note: Live Link is a built-in framework that streams data from external sources into the engine and maps it onto actors, with a generic role for non-animation data, extensible through plugins. Its documented sources are animation and tracking tools; connectors for industrial protocols or building systems and a path for a controller to be driven back are not part of it.

sources.title: Live Link in Unreal Engine
sources.quote: The purpose of Live Link is to provide a common interface for streaming and consuming animation data from external sources (for example, DDC tools or Mocap Servers) into Unreal Engine.

sources.title: Live Link in Unreal Engine
sources.quote: Supported Roles include Cameras, Lights, Characters, Transforms, and a Basic role (for generic data).

coverage.note: Unreal Engine has an analytics plugin whose Blueprint nodes record named events and pass them to a configured analytics provider, which is the studio-telemetry route; no learning-record format or xAPI output was found. Searched the Blueprint Analytics Plugin page on dev.epicgames.com and web searches limited to unrealengine.com and dev.epicgames.com for xAPI, SCORM, learning management system and analytics on 2026-10-20; found only provider-based event nodes. The unrealengine.com training and simulation page would not load without scripts, and the full Unreal documentation was not searched.

sources.title: Blueprint Analytics Plugin for Unreal Engine
sources.quote: A set of Blueprint nodes for communicating with analytics services.

coverage.note: Levels can be exported to USD through the USD Exporter plugin (level exporter options are documented), and the Migrate tool copies assets between Unreal projects. Neither is a whole-place export: the USD route covers level and asset content, the Migrate tool only moves Unreal-to-Unreal, and no documentation read states what survives if the host closes.

sources.title: ULevelExporterUSDOptions, Unreal Engine 5.8 Documentation
sources.quote: Options for exporting levels to USD format.

sources.title: Migrating Assets, Unreal Engine 5.8 Documentation
sources.quote: How to copy Assets from one project to another.

coverage.note: The Pixel Streaming plugin (and Pixel Streaming 2) runs a packaged Unreal application on a server or cloud machine and streams its rendered frames and audio to a browser over WebRTC, with mouse, touch, gamepad and XR input sent back. Headset (VR) streaming through WebXR is documented as a new, experimental feature; the pages state no pose-prediction or latency guarantee.

sources.title: Pixel Streaming in Unreal Engine (Unreal Engine 5.8 documentation)
sources.quote: Run your Unreal Engine application on a server in the cloud and stream its rendered frames and audio to browsers and mobile devices over WebRTC.

sources.title: Experimental Pixel Streaming Features (Unreal Engine 5.8 documentation)
sources.quote: Virtual Reality (VR) Pixel Streaming is a new feature that provides users with the means to connect to a VR-compatible application using Pixel Streaming. This allows users to enjoy a VR experience with their own headsets, without running a local application.

coverage.note: Unreal's augmented reality layer has a candidate-object asset and a tracked-object type for detecting a reference object, but the session configuration documents that feature as used by ARKit, so it covers Apple devices only, and the reference data is held as raw bytes rather than as a model file. No support for supplying a CAD or mesh model was found in this documentation.

sources.title: UARCandidateObject, Unreal Engine 5.8
sources.quote: An asset that points to an object to be detected in a scene

sources.title: ARSessionConfig, Unreal Python API 5.2
sources.quote: The list of candidate objects to search for in the scene. This feature is used by ARKit.
